pitch_detail.notes: P1 (5.11, about 50 m) starts by scrambling up and right to a pedestal with a single bolt; do not drift left toward the rap anchor, and belaying from the talus causes rope drag. P2 (5.11-, about 45 m) goes up and left to a rap anchor, then blocky ground to a tongue of clean rock, with loose blocks to watch for. P3 (5.12-, about 15 m) is a clean sculpted slab with a step-right crux, finishing on a sloping ledge under the overhanging Shield. Mostly less-than-vertical rock with some ledge scrambling.

P4 (5.12-, about 20 m) steps down right, then moves up jugs and trends left on airy edges to a stance in a dike; a straight-up direct variation is a closed project. P5 (5.13-, about 30 m) is the Dike pitch: the dike itself is about 5.11+, then a roughly V7 boulder crux on textureless pinches, then a 5.12 traverse right to a stance. P6 (5.11, about 30 m) is face climbing to a roof pull, then juggy sidepulls and edges to a corner belay.

P7 (5.12, about 30 m) follows a dihedral past a large rock scar, makes a hard step right on crimps, and rounds an arete to a sloping anchor stance before continuing through a roof to a second sloping stance; the line is widely rated one of the best pitches on the route. P8 (5.12, about 15 m) is a corner of laybacking and stemming to an airy lip, with the belay in an alcove. The key pinch through the roof is the crux of this section.

P9 (5.11-, about 30 m) climbs a left-facing corner using face holds, the crack and a juniper, then pulls right to a stance. P10 (5.11+, about 35 m) is a tricky slab to a good ledge that is a poor one-person bivy but suits a portaledge (extra bolts were added for that). P11 (5.12, about 36 m) is under-vertical climbing to a layback crux and the right edge of a small roof, then easier ground past a rap anchor to a ledge under the Big Overhang; loose rock on that ledge.

P12 (5.13-, about 45 m) goes straight up through choss below a small roof, boulders through a second roof, then trends left through slopers (about V6) to a shallow corner, passes a rap anchor, and finishes with a redpoint boulder (about V5) over a bulge; permadraws are in place and about five more draws are needed. P13 (5.12, about 20 m) is sidepulls and compression blocks to a boulder move at the lip. P14 (5.11-, about 20 m) is jugs and pockets past suspect rock, and P15 (5.12, about 35 m) is bulgy ground on unusual holds to a slightly overhanging crimp crux, then jugs left and up to a belay below cedars. Stick clips or rodeo-clipping the permadraws help on the hard sections of P14 and P15.

P16 (5.8, about 65 m) is hands on rock and feet on cedars to a rap anchor, then a corner to a stance under a slab. P17 (5.9, about 70 m) is easy slab to a rock with a rap anchor, over it to cracks and trees, right to regain rock, then heather and trees past a tree rap anchor to a two-bolt anchor just below the buttress summit; a few feet of simul-climbing may be needed. Minimally cleaned, with loose rock on the ledges.

review.changed: Kept the six stored section labels and wrote per-pitch detail (grades and approximate lengths as stated in the route description, put in notes because the page calls them approximations rather than measurements) inside each. No rappel_detail written: the sources give rappel OPTIONS (skip the P12/P13 belays via dedicated anchors, skip the near-P11-top anchor with an 80 m rope, rap the Dike pitch via its own anchor, rap P1 straight down to an intermediate rap and the talus) but no numbered station list or per-rappel lengths, so a station-by-station table would be invented. The stored rappels text already covers the single-70 m-rope point.
review.other_findings: Route page says 17 pitches while the AAJ article says 21 (stored beta already explains 17 linked vs 21 split). AAJ puts the 5.13 range at pitches 6 and 14 and the crux at 13 on its own numbering, which does not match the route page's numbering (crux 5.13- at P5 and P12); numbering differs by source, not reconciled.

pitch_detail.notes: Where the lower ridge steepens into upper 5th class at a few trees, traverse left onto the more exposed side of the ridge. Find a snag beside a vertical #3-size crack. Climb cracks from the snag, including a short hand crack with 5.7 moves, to a belay just below the roof.

The 'Pac Man' pitch. Traverse out right under the roof, passing beneath its right side (going up and left over it is harder), and continue about 50 ft beyond. This pitch takes the most gear, and some parties find it the hardest. Above, scramble roughly ten minutes of class 3 up the ridge to the next steepening. The way on is not obvious here, and the gully alongside is loose.

Start on the steepening ground and follow cracks, belaying where comfortable or at the base of a 10-inch-wide crack. Parties often link pitches 3 to 5 into two. Some belay 20–30 ft past the fixed rap anchors for better stances.
Short start up the 10-inch crack, with gear in cracks to its left. Above it, follow finger and hand cracks past a shallow gully and some bushes to a belay on a flat section.

Two options at the start: stay in the corner to the right the whole way, or take the middle cracks straight up to a tree. Either way, lieback the corner the tree grows in. Above the corner, easier ground leads to the next steepening of the ridge. Much of this pitch is easier than the others.
Follow cracks up to lower-angle ground and belay after about 140 ft, below the final headwall, which has a #3-size crack out to the left. Pitches 6 and 7 are the best-regarded on the route.

Short, excellent leaning crack on the left that starts at #3 size and gets smaller, the trickiest section of the route; only two or three pieces. The easier option is the blocky trough and gully to its right: walk a short ledge to an exposed step, then climb a second steep groove.

About 200–300 ft of class 3 along the crest, with an exposed 4th-class move near the summit. Topping out commits the party to descending the loose gully climber's right of the route. From the summit one rappel reaches that gully.

review.changed: Stored table was already close to the only full description; kept all labels and only sharpened P5 (two start options) and P7 (crack tapers from #3, hardest part). No rappel_detail: the sources only say the route is descended by rappel on a 60 m rope (some raps stretch it), with fixed anchors near P3, and that one rappel from the top reaches the gully; no station-by-station list was found. Mountaineers.org pages 403'd, so no second full source read.
review.other_findings: Route page header says 6 pitches (7th optional); stored pitches=7 is consistent. Stored rappels text says about nine rappels the whole way; that figure was not confirmed on the page I could read.

pitch_detail.notes: The first bolt blends into the rock and is hard to spot. Climb just above a left-trending overlap, then up past three bolts on thin, exciting face climbing to the anchor. Short runouts, and some poor rock between bolts.

Climb past two bolts to reach a crack. At the third bolt, traverse right and follow easier cracks to the anchor. Pitches 1 and 2 can each be rappelled with a 70 m rope. Short runouts and some poor rock.

The long bolted pitch. A hard start for about the first 20 ft, then moderate 5.7–5.8 face and slab climbing to a tree anchor. The webbing at the tree may need replacing, so inspect it before trusting it.

Enjoyable cracks graded 5.6–5.7 lead to the top. Belay from a gear anchor or a tree. To descend, scramble back to the top of pitch 3 and rappel the route. A standard rack to 2 inches works, with extra runners for rope drag.

skip_reasons.wa_summertime: Route page's description is already what is stored (P1 bolts to chains past the tops of Caravan and Django, P2 corner/slab, crux P3 5.11c, easy 5.10 finish); nothing further to add. No descent info beyond chains at several points, so no rappel table.
